newsitem.title: UK: Slovenia defends foreign investment controls.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia defends foreign investment controls.

text.p: Slovenia defended controversial restrictions on foreign investors' ability to trade its securities but a senior central banker accused the country's banks of exploiting the new system.

In a move which some analysts called discriminatory, the Bank of Slovenia ruled in February that international portfolio investors could trade only through special accounts at one of Slovenia's 14 fully licensed banks.
The banks have signalled they may charge up to 12 percent in handling fees.

Central bank deputy governor Andrej Rant said at a presentation at the annual meeting of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) on Saturday that the step had been necessary because of the potentially destabilising effects of the large foreign inflows.
"Our experience of foreign capital was very unpleasant. In 1996, a direct consequence of increased foreign capital inflows was the bankruptcy of one bank," he said.
However, he acknowledged that the Slovenian banks were charging too much to handle the securities trade.
"We think very strongly that the banks exaggerate the price of safety. We think that a fair price has to be established that is accepted and understood by all participants in the market," Rant said.

Slovenia has been one of the big success stories in the transformation of East European contralised economies to market democracies. In the first six weeks of 1997, portfolio funds invested $30 million -- almost half the 1996 total.
But governments and central banks across the region fear the possible effect of hot money quickly entering and leaving the economy.
Rant said the high volume of foreign investment could impact the money supply and the tolar's exchange rate and that this could hit the real and financial sectors.
"It could be a cause of major problems which could arise in the banking sector," he said.
